a2a.def: Google's open protocol for AI agents to find and message each other. Introduced April 2025, now at the Linux Foundation.

signedoffer.def: An offer both sides sign with keys, so the promise can be proved later. Illustrative; no standard yet.

pKarpathy.def: AI researcher, an OpenAI founding member and former head of AI at Tesla, who coined “vibe coding” in February 2025.

pHoward.def: Co-founder of fast.ai and Answer.AI, who proposed llms.txt in September 2024.

computeruse.def: An AI model operating a computer: reading the screen, clicking, typing. Anthropic, public beta, October 2024.

operator.def: OpenAI's browser-using agent, launched as a research preview on 23 January 2025.

webmcp.def: Proposed standard letting a page hand agents named tools to call. Early preview in Chrome 146, origin trial in 149.

mcp.def: Model Context Protocol: Anthropic's open standard (Nov 2024) for plugging AI models into tools and data.

llmstxt.def: A markdown map of a site for AI models, at /llms.txt. Proposed 2024; big AI firms haven't committed to it.

aiov.def: AI-written summaries at the top of Google results, rolled out to everyone in the US from 14 May 2024.

zeroclick.def: A search that ends on the results page because the answer is already there, so no site gets a visit.

acp.def: Agentic Commerce Protocol, from OpenAI and Stripe: lets an AI agent check out for you. Powers Instant Checkout.

ap2.def: Agent Payments Protocol, Google, September 2025. Signed “mandates” prove what you let an agent buy.

x402.def: Coinbase's protocol (May 2025) that revives HTTP 402 so agents can pay per request.

h402.def: “Payment Required”: an HTTP status code reserved since the 1990s and barely used, until now.

webbotauth.def: Bots sign their requests with a published key, so sites can check who's really knocking.

payperCrawl.def: Cloudflare's private beta (1 July 2025) letting sites allow, block or charge AI crawlers, using HTTP 402 responses.

robots.def: A text file telling crawlers what they may fetch. A 1994 convention, an official standard since 2022.

aicrawler.def: A bot that downloads pages to train or feed AI models, not to send you visitors.

ondevice.def: An AI model running on your own machine, so your data never leaves it.

nano.def: Google's smallest Gemini model, downloaded by Chrome to run its built-in AI APIs locally.

builtinai.def: Chrome APIs such as Summarizer, Translator and Language Detector, available in stable Chrome from version 138 (mid-2025).

genui.def: Screens assembled by a model on the fly, for one person and one task.

vibecoding.def: Describing an app and letting AI write the code, mostly unread. Named by Andrej Karpathy, February 2025.

agent.def: An AI that takes actions, not just answers: it plans, uses tools or a browser, and keeps going.

llm.def: Large language model: a neural network trained on huge amounts of text. The engine inside chatbots and agents.

aibrowser.def: A browser built around an assistant that can read the open tabs and act on pages for you.

promptinj.def: Hidden text on a page that tries to give an AI agent new orders. Why agents ask before risky steps.

a11ytree.def: The browser's structured view of a page (roles, names, states) built for screen readers. Agents often read it too.

origintrial.def: A way for sites to try an experimental Chrome feature in production for a limited time.

instantcheckout.def: Buying inside ChatGPT, launched 29 September 2025 for US users, starting with Etsy sellers. Built on the Agentic Commerce Protocol.

comet.def: Perplexity's AI browser, released 9 July 2025 for top-tier subscribers and made free for everyone on 2 October 2025.

atlas.def: OpenAI's AI browser, launched for macOS on 21 October 2025.

dia.def: An AI browser from The Browser Company, early access from June 2025. Atlassian bought the company.

autobrowse.def: Gemini in Chrome's agent mode (2026). It clicks through sites in its own tab and pauses before buying.

claudechrome.def: Anthropic's extension that lets Claude read and act on web pages. Generally available since August 2026.

anthropic.def: An AI company that makes the Claude models; it introduced computer use and MCP.

openai.def: The AI company behind ChatGPT; it launched Operator and Instant Checkout.

perplexity.def: An AI answer-engine company; it makes the Comet browser.

cloudflare.def: A huge network in front of millions of sites, so its defaults decide how bots get treated.

stripe.def: A payments company; it co-developed the Agentic Commerce Protocol with OpenAI.

coinbase.def: A cryptocurrency exchange; it published the x402 payment protocol in May 2025.

pew.def: A nonpartisan US research organisation. Its July 2025 study tracked 68,879 real Google searches by 900 adults.

pTBL.def: British computer scientist who invented the web at CERN in 1989–90 and founded the W3C in 1994.

pSendall.def: Tim's manager at CERN. He wrote “vague but exciting” on the proposal and let Tim build it anyway.

pCailliau.def: Belgian engineer at CERN who co-wrote the 1990 web proposal and championed it inside the lab.

pPellow.def: Maths student on placement at CERN who wrote the line-mode browser in 1990–91.

pKunz.def: SLAC physicist who set up the first web server in North America, in December 1991.

pAndreessen.def: Co-wrote Mosaic at NCSA as a student, then co-founded Netscape. Later a venture capitalist.

pBina.def: NCSA programmer who co-wrote Mosaic with Marc Andreessen and then co-founded Netscape.

pLerdorf.def: Danish-Canadian programmer who created PHP in 1995.

pEich.def: Created JavaScript at Netscape in 1995. Later co-founded Mozilla and Brave.

pLie.def: Norwegian web pioneer who proposed CSS at CERN in 1994, later CTO of the Opera browser.

pGarrett.def: User-experience designer at Adaptive Path who named Ajax in a February 2005 essay.

pResig.def: Created jQuery in 2006, then worked at Mozilla and Khan Academy.

pDHH.def: Danish programmer, known as DHH, who created Ruby on Rails at 37signals.

pDahl.def: Created Node.js in 2009, then Deno in 2018 to fix what he regretted about Node.

pYou.def: Independent developer who created Vue (2014) and the Vite build tool (2020).

pRauch.def: Created Socket.IO and founded Vercel, the company behind Next.js.

pHarris.def: Created Svelte and the Rollup bundler while building interactive news graphics.

pQSF.def: Cambridge computer scientist who, with Paul Jardetzky, wired up the Trojan Room coffee-pot camera in 1991.

homepage.def: A personal website, usually a few hand-written HTML pages about you, your pets and your favourite links.

sharedhost.def: One server shared by hundreds of sites, each in a folder. Cheap, and home to most 90s pages.

crawler.def: A search engine's program that downloads pages to index them. Early crawlers didn't run JavaScript, so client-rendered pages looked empty.

infinite.def: Loading more items automatically as you near the bottom, so the page never ends. Everywhere from about 2010.

production.def: The live environment real users hit, as opposed to a staging or preview deployment.

trojan.def: A coffee pot at Cambridge University's Computer Lab. On camera from 1991, on the web 1993–2001.

webcam.def: A camera that publishes images to the web. The Trojan Room coffee pot is usually called the first famous one.

nextstep.def: The operating system on NeXT computers. It later became the core of Mac OS X.

nextcube.def: A black workstation from NeXT, Steve Jobs' company after Apple. The first web server ran on one.

wwwapp.def: The first browser, which could also edit pages. Written by Tim Berners-Lee in 1990.

linemode.def: A text-only browser by Nicola Pellow that ran on any terminal. Links were numbers you typed.

terminal.def: A screen and keyboard with no real computer inside. It showed text from a shared machine.

cern.def: The European Organization for Nuclear Research, the particle physics lab near Geneva where the web was invented.

slac.def: Stanford Linear Accelerator Center in California. It ran the first web server outside Europe, from December 1991.

w3c.def: The World Wide Web Consortium, founded by Tim Berners-Lee to write the web's standards.

arpanet.def: The US research network that grew into the internet. It sent its first message in 1969.

httpd.def: HTTP daemon: the web server program. CERN httpd came first; NCSA HTTPd followed and Apache grew out of it.

ncsa.def: National Center for Supercomputing Applications at the University of Illinois. It built Mosaic and the NCSA HTTPd server.

netscape.def: The browser that ruled the mid-90s. Netscape's 1995 IPO kicked off the dot-com boom.

ie.def: Microsoft's browser. Bundled with Windows, it won the first browser war, then stood still for years. Retired in 2022.

browserwars.def: Netscape against Internet Explorer, roughly 1995–2001. Both raced to add incompatible features; IE won by shipping with Windows.

sun.def: Sun Microsystems, maker of Java. The JavaScript name came from a deal with Sun.

geocities.def: Free homepages sorted into themed “neighbourhoods”. Yahoo bought it in 1999 and shut it down in 2009.

webring.def: A loop of sites on one topic, linked by prev and next buttons. 90s discovery, before good search.

guestbook.def: A page where visitors left a public message, usually run by a CGI script.

hitcounter.def: A CGI script that counted page loads and showed the total as odometer digits.

y2k.def: The fear that two-digit years would break software on 1 January 2000. Years of fixes meant little did.

dotcom.def: The late-90s internet investment frenzy. Tech stocks peaked in March 2000, then lost about 78%.

flash.def: A browser plug-in for animation, games and video, huge in the 2000s. Adobe ended support at the end of 2020.

gmail.def: Google's webmail, launched 1 April 2004 with 1 GB of storage and a no-reload interface.

gmaps.def: Google's 2005 map you could drag smoothly, loading tiles in the background with Ajax.

web20.def: A label, popularised by Tim O'Reilly's 2004 conference, for sites built on user content, sharing and rich in-browser interaction.

beta.def: In the 2000s products stayed labelled “beta” for years. Gmail only dropped the badge in July 2009.

blog.def: Short for weblog: a personal site of dated posts, newest first.

rss.def: An XML feed of a site's latest posts that readers could subscribe to in a feed reader.

django.def: A Python web framework built at the Lawrence Journal-World newspaper in Kansas.

aws.def: Amazon Web Services: renting Amazon's infrastructure by the hour. S3 and EC2 launched in 2006.

useast.def: AWS's oldest, busiest region, in Virginia. When it has a bad day, the internet notices.

iphone.def: Apple's 2007 phone with a full web browser. It made the mobile web mainstream, and never supported Flash.

heroku.def: A platform where deploying meant running git push heroku master. It made PaaS popular.

backbone.def: A small library by Jeremy Ashkenas that gave browser apps models, views and a router.

angularjs.def: Google's framework with two-way data binding and templates full of '{{' '}}'. Rewritten from scratch as Angular in 2016.

jsconf.def: A community-run series of JavaScript conferences, where Node.js and React were both first shown.

jsx.def: React's syntax for writing HTML-like tags inside JavaScript. It compiles to plain function calls.

leftpad.def: An 11-line npm package. Unpublished in March 2016, it broke thousands of builds.

responsive.def: One layout that adapts to any screen with CSS media queries. Named by Ethan Marcotte in 2010.

flat.def: The early-2010s move from glossy, realistic textures to plain shapes and colour. Google's Material Design (2014) added paper-like shadows back.

kubernetes.def: Google's open-source system for running containers across a cluster: scheduling, restarts and scaling.

deno.def: A JavaScript and TypeScript runtime by Ryan Dahl: secure by default, with TypeScript built in.

vue.def: A front-end framework by Evan You: HTML templates plus reactive data, adoptable one page at a time.

nextjs.def: Vercel's React framework for server rendering, routing and static generation.

svelte.def: A framework by Rich Harris that compiles components to plain JavaScript at build time, with no runtime library.

socketio.def: A library by Guillermo Rauch for real-time two-way messages between browser and server.

rollup.def: A JavaScript module bundler by Rich Harris, known for tree-shaking unused code.

vite.def: Evan You's build tool (2020) with a near-instant dev server.

typescript.def: Microsoft's typed superset of JavaScript. It compiles to plain JS and became the default for large front-end codebases.

monorepo.def: One repository holding many apps and packages, so they share code and change together.

jamstack.def: JavaScript, APIs and Markup: pre-built pages on a CDN, with dynamic parts handled by APIs. Coined at Netlify.

postgres.def: PostgreSQL, an open-source relational database descended from Berkeley's POSTGRES project.

edgefn.def: A small serverless function deployed to many locations at once, run in whichever one is closest to the user.

rsc.def: React components that run only on the server and ship none of their own code to the browser.

xhr.def: The browser API behind Ajax. Microsoft shipped it in Internet Explorer 5; the other browsers copied it.

tcpip.def: The internet's base protocols: IP moves packets, TCP makes them a reliable stream. Standard since 1983.

lamp.def: Linux, Apache, MySQL and PHP (or Perl, or Python). The free default stack for 2000s websites.

node.def: JavaScript outside the browser, on Chrome's V8 engine, with non-blocking I/O. One language on both sides of the wire.

rails.def: A full-stack MVC framework in Ruby. Made “convention over configuration” and database migrations mainstream.

jquery.def: A library that hid browser differences behind one $() function for selecting elements, events, animation and Ajax.

js.def: The browser's scripting language, written by Brendan Eich at Netscape. Standardised as ECMAScript in 1997.

ajax.def: Asynchronous JavaScript and XML: fetch data in the background and update part of the page without a full reload.

json.def: A small text format for data, popularised by Douglas Crockford. It replaced XML for most APIs.

rest.def: A style for APIs: resources live at URLs, and you act on them with GET, POST and DELETE.

http.def: HyperText Transfer Protocol. How browsers and servers talk: GET a URL, get back a status code, headers and a body.

html.def: HyperText Markup Language. Plain text with tags like '<'h1> and '<'a> that give a page its structure and its links.

url.def: Uniform Resource Locator. An address like https://example.com/page: the protocol, the host, then the path.

hypertext.def: Text with links you can follow to other text. Ted Nelson coined the word; the web made it global.

newsgroup.def: A Usenet discussion group, the internet's message boards since 1980. alt.hypertext was one of thousands.

mosaic.def: The 1993 NCSA browser that put images inline with text and made the web popular.

cgi.def: Common Gateway Interface. The web server starts a program for each request and sends back whatever it prints.

perl.def: Larry Wall's text-processing language, the default choice for CGI scripts in the 90s.

php.def: Rasmus Lerdorf's 1995 language: code mixed into HTML, run by the server on every request.

isp.def: Internet service provider. The company whose modems you dialled into to get online.

dialup.def: Getting online with a phone call. Nobody could use the phone while you surfed.

baud.def: Kilobits per second. A 28.8k modem moved about 3.6 KB a second, on a good day.

modem.def: Modulator-demodulator. Turns digital data into audio tones that travel down a phone line, and back again.

colo.def: Renting rack space, power and bandwidth in someone else's data center for servers you bought and own.

apache.def: Grew out of patches to the NCSA web server and was the most-used web server from 1996 into the 2010s.

mysql.def: A fast, free relational database. The M in LAMP.

memcached.def: An in-memory key-value cache written for LiveJournal. It saves the database from answering the same query again and again.

lb.def: A box or program that spreads incoming requests across several identical servers.

css.def: Cascading Style Sheets: rules for how HTML should look, kept apart from the content. Proposed in 1994, CSS1 in 1996.

mvc.def: Model–View–Controller. Split an app into data, display, and the code connecting them. From Smalltalk.

vps.def: Virtual private server. One physical machine split into several virtual ones, each with its own OS and root access.

ec2.def: Amazon's rentable virtual servers, started with an API call. Launched 2006.

s3.def: Amazon Simple Storage Service. Put any file at a URL and pay per gigabyte. Launched March 2006.

paas.def: Platform as a service: you push code, the platform runs it. Heroku made it famous.

cdn.def: Content delivery network: copies of your files around the world, served from the closest one.

spa.def: Single-page app: one HTML page whose JavaScript draws every screen and fetches its own data.

csr.def: Client-side rendering: the browser builds the page with JavaScript. Fast later, slow to start.

ssr.def: Server-side rendering: the server sends finished HTML. Fast first paint, easy for search engines.

ssg.def: Static site generation. Pages are rendered to HTML files at build time and served from a CDN.

isr.def: Incremental static regeneration. Static pages rebuilt in the background after a time limit or on demand, without a full redeploy.

hydration.def: Running a server-rendered page's JavaScript in the browser so it attaches event handlers and becomes interactive.

bundle.def: All of an app's JavaScript squashed into a few files by a build tool.

npm.def: The Node package manager and registry. One command installs a package and everything it depends on.

v8.def: Chrome's JavaScript engine. It compiles JS to machine code, which made JavaScript fast enough for big apps and servers.

react.def: A UI library from Facebook. Describe the UI for a given state and React works out the DOM changes.

docker.def: Packages an app with its whole environment into an image that runs the same on any machine.

serverless.def: Upload a function; the platform runs it per request and bills per call. Servers still exist, unseen.

git.def: Sending commits to a shared repository. Platforms hook in so every push triggers a build, tests and a deploy.

api.def: A defined way for one program to ask another for data or actions. On the web, usually HTTP.

dns.def: Domain Name System. Turns names like example.com into IP addresses via a worldwide hierarchy of servers.

ttfb.def: Time to first byte: how long after the request the first byte of the response arrives.

latency.def: How long a round trip takes. Light in fibre covers about 200 km per millisecond, so distance always costs something.

streaming.def: Sending a response in pieces as they're ready, so the browser can show the first parts early.

edge.def: Running code in data centers close to users, instead of in one central region.

browser.def: The program that fetches pages over HTTP and draws them. The first one, WorldWideWeb, was also an editor.

server.def: A program, and the machine running it, that answers requests. The first web server was CERN httpd.
